item.title: Directed Evolution of the Cbx1 Chromodomain Generates a High-Affinity Trimethyllysine-Binding Variant
item.description:
Abstract
Directed evolution is a powerful and versatile strategy for engineering proteins with enhanced affinity and tailored molecular recognition properties. Here, we applied phage display-guided directed evolution to enhance the binding of the wild-type Cbx1 chromodomain (Cbx1-CD) to an H3K9me3-containing peptide. Screening a soft-randomized library targeting residues surrounding the aromatic cage yielded C29, which bound the H3K9me3 peptide with a KD of 57 nM and exhibited an approximately 14-fold lower dissociation rate constant than Cbx1-CD. Across an H3K9me3-derived alanine-scanning series and a peptide panel, C29 showed stronger binding signals than Cbx1-CD for multiple peptides containing trimethyllysine (Kme3), suggesting lower flanking-sequence dependence for C29 than for Cbx1-CD. An AlphaFold3 model of the C29-H3K9me3 complex suggested local changes in the hydrophobic and electrostatic environment surrounding the Kme3-binding pocket, providing a mechanistic hypothesis for C29’s enhanced affinity and reduced flanking-sequence dependence. When two Kme3-containing peptides were spiked into a 100-fold molar excess of unmodified background peptides, C29-conjugated beads effectively enriched both Kme3 peptides relative to the unmodified background. These findings define C29 as a high-affinity Kme3-binding Cbx1 chromodomain variant and support its further evaluation as an affinity reagent for Kme3-containing peptide enrichment.

item.title: Small-Molecule Inhibitors of Cholesterol Sulfotransferase as Immunomodulatory Agents
item.description:
Abstract
Though immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy has been a promising advance in cancer treatment, response rates to ICB are low owing to other mechanisms that cancers employ to evade the immune system. SULT2B1b is an enzyme known to produce cholesterol sulfate (CS), an immunosuppressive metabolite that inhibits T-cell migration. Cancers expressing high levels of SULT2B1b thus generate a tumor microenvironment that excludes T cells, which leads to increased tumor growth and renders ICB therapy ineffective. Here, we identify a novel class of azasteroid SULT2B1b inhibitors with greater potency and selectivity than previously identified compounds. X-ray co-crystal structures indicate that these inhibitors bind in a conformation different from that of native substrates, enabling inhibition without acting as a substrate. Additionally, these new compounds effectively reduce CS levels in tumors in mice and, as such, have potential as cancer therapeutics in combination with ICB therapy.

item.title: Oxidized 5-Methylcytosines and Nucleosome Architecture Cooperatively Influence Thymine DNA Glycosylase Activity
item.description:
Abstract
Active DNA demethylation is a fundamental epigenetic process in which the iterative oxidation of 5-methylcytosine (5mC) by TET dioxygenases generates diverse combinations of oxidized 5-methylcytosines within CpG dinucleotides before their excision by thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG). Although heterogeneous CpG oxidation states are expected to arise frequently during this process, how the modification state of the opposing cytosine influences TDG activity remains poorly understood. Here, we developed a chemically defined panel of CpG substrates containing cytosine, 5mC, 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), 5-formylcytosine (5fC), and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC) opposite a target 5fC and systematically examined TDG-mediated excision in both naked DNA and nucleosome core particles (NCPs). In naked DNA, opposing-strand cytosine modifications exerted only modest effects on TDG activity when a single excisable base was present within the CpG dyad, whereas dual-substrate CpGs exhibited unexpected differences in strand utilization. In contrast, nucleosome assembly profoundly altered TDG activity, revealing modification-dependent effects that were largely absent in naked DNA and dramatically redistributing strand utilization within dual-substrate CpGs. Together, these findings demonstrate that the oxidation-state composition of a CpG dyad and nucleosome architecture cooperatively regulate TDG activity, establishing heterogeneous CpG oxidation states as functionally distinct substrates for TDG and providing a biochemical framework for understanding how chromatin structure regulates active DNA demethylation.

item.title: G-Tract Length Shapes the Fate of G-Quadruplexes
item.description:
Abstract
Guanine (G)-rich DNA sequences can form unusual secondary structures known as G-quadruplexes (or G4s). The stability of these structures, whose folding is mainly driven by the formation and stacking of G-quartets, is influenced by several factors, foremost among them the nature of the sequence itself, particularly the nucleobases flanking the G-tracts, and the loops connecting them. A considerable effort has been devoted to understanding how the size, position, and composition of each loop and flanking sequences affect the stability of the resulting G4 fold. However, most of these studies have been restricted to sequences forming a three G-quartet G4 core. To better understand how the length of the G-tracts (from three to five Gs) and loops (from one to seven nucleotides) act in concert, we studied a set of 261 different sequences covering different possible combinations. A systematic biophysical analysis suggests that sequences with longer G-tracts tend to form more stable G4s, but also a mixture of species; it further shows that loop composition and position also influence the topology and stability of the resulting G4s. Collectively, this work provides an unprecedented view on how G4-forming sequences fold upon themselves and of the structural features that govern the stability of the resulting G4s.

item.title: Conjugation of a Cell-Penetrating Peptide to the Lasso Peptides Citrocin and Microcin J25 Enhances Antimicrobial Activity
item.description:
Abstract
A subset of lasso peptides function as antibiotics against Gram-negative bacteria by inhibition of the bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP), including microcin J25 (MccJ25) and citrocin. These peptides interact with specific transporters in the inner and outer membranes of bacteria to gain access to the cytoplasm. The reliance on transporters limits the breadth of spectrum of these lasso peptide antibiotics and opens up paths to drug resistance. Here, we detail a strategy to overcome the transport limitations of lasso peptides: covalent conjugation of the lasso peptide to a cell penetrating peptide (CPP). Citrocin-CPP and MccJ25-CPP conjugates were synthesized by attaching the CPP to the loop of the lasso peptide and tested for antimicrobial activity against the ESKAPE pathogens. Citrocin-CPP and MccJ25-CPP have antimicrobial activity against all four Gram-negative ESKAPE pathogens, a broader spectrum of activity than the parent lasso peptides. Citrocin-CPP and MccJ25-CPP also exhibit more potent activity than the parent lasso peptides, with minimum inhibitory concentrations in the high nanomolar to single micromolar range. The uptake of citrocin-CPP and MccJ25-CPP was also studied in Escherichia coli revealing that the conjugates are internalized via both transporter-dependent and transporter-independent pathways.

item.title: Pharmacological ON/OFF Regulation of CAR T Cells through Estrogen Receptor-Based Stabilization and Targeted Degradation
item.description:
Abstract
Regulation of therapeutic cell response is important for safe and effective therapy, particularly for immunotherapy. Ideally, the regulators should be based on human proteins using compounds that have already been approved for human use. Regulation of protein degradation by small molecules enables fast cellular response and a small genetic footprint of genetic constructs. Here, we present a clinically compatible strategy for reversible pharmacological control of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell function using human estrogen receptor (ER)-based degron domains and FDA-approved small molecules. By fusing tamoxifen-responsive ER ligand-binding domains to CARs, we generate ligand-inducible ON-switch CARs whose stability, signaling, and effector functions are precisely controlled by 4-hydroxytamoxifen. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ER-tagged CARs can be selectively degraded using the FDA-approved ER-targeting PROTAC ARV-471, establishing a complementary OFF-switch mechanism that suppresses CAR expression and effector function. Notably, these results expand the ON-OFF switch platform for post-translational control of therapeutic proteins, offering new opportunities to improve the safety and precision of cellular immunotherapies.

item.title: Site-Selective Bioconjugations of Distinct Methionine Residues in a Protein via Reactivity-Based Reagent Control
item.description:
Abstract
The reaction of thioethers in biological macromolecules with oxaziridines enables their functionalization with moieties having utility in both basic and applied science. Exploitation of that reaction has advantages over common bioconjugations due to the relatively low abundance and weak reactivity of thioethers. Herein, we report a novel and improved route to 1-ureal piperidine,3-aryl oxaziridines that enables the preparation of bioconjugation reagents that are either electronically activated or deactivated. We leveraged the differential reactivities of the oxaziridine reagents and engineered methionine residues in distinct environments within a therapeutically relevant antibody fragment (Fab) to effect site-selective bioconjugations. We capitalized on this novel means of kinetic resolution to effect dual functionalization of a HER2-targeted Fab with distinct fluorophores for imaging receptor internalization. This work broadens the scope of what is possible in bioconjugations of thioethers and demonstrates that site-selective bioconjugations of the same residue at more than one site in a protein can be realized via reactivity-based reagent control.

item.title: A Biocompatible Cu(I)-Catalyzed Click Chemistry Framework for Long-Term Cell Tracking
item.description:
Abstract
Cellular immunotherapies have transformed oncologic treatment in recent years, yet the inability to monitor cell migration post-transfusion remains a significant barrier to their development. Here, we explore the feasibility of a non-invasive cell-tracking method utilizing Cu(I)-catalyzed click chemistry in which cells are first labeled with alkynes and, after 1–2 weeks, are selectively targeted via an azide-conjugated fluorescent probe. We developed Click1, a novel tris-Cu-chelating azide capable of a rapid, robust click reaction directly on live cell surfaces with minimal cytotoxicity. When paired with Click1, two distinct alkyne-labeling reagents, N-(4-pentynoyl)-mannosamine-tetraacylated (Ac4ManNAl) and propargyl choline, were capable of detecting human T cells for over two weeks. Our findings elucidate the metabolic turnover of biochemical handles in primary immune cells, providing a potential framework for long-term cell tracking in immunotherapies.

item.title: High-Throughput Screening Identifies Small-Molecule Inhibitors of the Tau-LRP1 Interaction
item.description:
Abstract
The cellular uptake and propagation of tau are central features of tauopathies, including Alzheimer’s disease, and are mediated by the endocytic receptor low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1). While prior studies have implicated LRP1 in tau binding and internalization, the biochemical features of this interaction and its suitability for therapeutic targeting remain incompletely defined. Here, we establish a quantitative and scalable framework to interrogate the tau-LRP1 interaction and identify small-molecule modulators. We engineered and purified the LRP1 ligand-binding domain 4 (BD4), a key region mediating tau interaction, and developed multiple orthogonal assays, including fluorescence polarization, split luciferase complementation, and time-resolved FRET, to measure LRP1-BD4 interactions with tau and a known peptide ligand. Across assay formats, we observe consistent binding affinities in the nanomolar range and demonstrate competitive displacement by tau, receptor-associated protein (RAP), and a peptide ligand, supporting overlapping binding interfaces. Leveraging these platforms, we performed small-molecule high-throughput screening and identified a set of candidate inhibitors of the LRP1-BD4-tau interaction. Selected compounds reduced tau uptake in a cellular assay, phenocopying competitive inhibition by tau and a peptide ligand. Together, these studies define the LRP1-BD4-tau interaction as a biochemically tractable and druggable interface and establish an integrated discovery pipeline linking mechanistic characterization to functional cellular outcomes. This work provides a foundation for the development of therapeutic strategies targeting LRP1-mediated tau uptake.

item.title: A Modular Optogenetic Split-Small GTPase Platform Reveals Long-Range RhoA Signaling
item.description:
Abstract
Small GTPases are critical regulators of cellular processes such as cell migration. However, no generalizable method exists for directly controlling their activity with subcellular precision, limiting the ability to dissect long-range signaling effects. To address this, we pair fragmented small GTPases with improved light-inducible dimerization (iLID) domains, optimizing for low dark-state background and efficient light-induced reassembly, affording spLIT-small GTPases. Demonstrating modularity, we control filopodia formation (spLIT-Cdc42), cell movement (spLIT-Rac1), and membrane retraction (spLIT-RhoA) with subcellular precision. Applying this platform to long-range signaling, we provide the first demonstration that localized RhoA activation is sufficient to drive membrane retraction at the opposite cell pole, with a directional dependence set by actin cytoskeleton polarization, a result inaccessible to global perturbations used previously. These results suggest a mechanism for coordinated establishment of cell polarity and highlight spLIT-small GTPases as a versatile platform for the direct, spatial control of small GTPase signaling in living cells.

item.title: Characterization of Chromone Biosynthetic Pathway Reveals a Noncanonical Mode of Fungal Polyketide Cyclization
item.description:
Abstract
Fungal nonreducing polyketide synthases (NRPKSs) produce therapeutically and ecologically important aromatic polyketides. The product template (PT) domain of fungal NRPKSs catalyzes the regioselective aldol cyclization of the reactive poly-β-ketone chain during polyketide maturation and is essential for product fidelity of the NRPKSs. Herein, we discovered the fungal NRPKS MecA of which the polyketide cyclization steps do not involve a functional PT domain. MecA is encoded in the biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) responsible for the formation of 5-hydroxy-7-methoxy-2,3-dimethylchromone (1) from the biocontrol fungus Trichoderma afroharzianum T22. Heterologous expression and in vitro enzymatic assays fully established a biosynthetic pathway of 1 that involves three enzymes: MecA, dehydratase MecB, and methyltransferase MecC. The PT domain of MecA does not contain the conserved catalytic histidine that is essential for aldol cyclization activity. Consistent with the predicted inactive PT domain, MecA was demonstrated to catalyze a C1–C6 Claisen condensation as the first cyclization step of the pentaketide precursor, instead of the canonical aldol cyclization. Reconstitution of dissected MecA domains further demonstrated that the activity of MecA was not affected when the PT domain was removed. A Claisen Cyclase (CLC) domain that typically catalyzes Claisen cyclization in NRPKSs is also absent in MecA, implying the observed C1–C6 cyclization step is catalyzed by the remaining domains. This work contributes to the diversity of NRPKS cyclization chemistry and enables further genome mining and engineering of NRPKSs that may lead to biosynthesis of new aromatic polyketides.

item.title: Improving PROTAC-Mediated Degradation in Mouse Models: BRD9 as a Case Study
item.description:
Abstract
Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) have emerged as powerful chemical tools and therapeutics, yet their translation from preclinical models to humans remains inconsistent. Here, we systematically evaluate the activity of BRD9-targeting PROTACs in human and mouse systems to elucidate a key limitation in preclinical studies. Widely used CRBN- and VHL-recruiting degraders, including dBRD9 and VZ185, exhibit markedly reduced potency in mouse cells despite high sequence conservation of BRD9. Mechanistic interrogation reveals that species-specific differences in E3 ligases, particularly the Crbn I391 residue and structural variations in VHL, likely impair productive ternary complex formation. Expression of human CRBN or VHL, or introduction of the CrbnI391V mutation, increases degradation potency in mouse cells. Importantly, in vivo studies demonstrate enhanced BRD9 degradation in CrbnI391V mice using clinically relevant degraders. These findings highlight a critical barrier in PROTAC evaluation and establish humanized E3 ligase models as tools for more accurate assessment of on-target efficacy and toxicity.

item.title: Chemical and Genetically Encoded Strategies for Spatiotemporal Control of Lipid Generation in Living Cells
item.description:
Abstract
Mammalian cells synthesize thousands of distinct lipids, and lipid metabolism fundamentally influences signaling in both homeostatic and disease states. Despite considerable interest in the biological functions of diverse lipid species, direct study of their effects in biological systems has historically been limited by a lack of methods to modulate discrete lipid species with precise spatiotemporal control. Several efforts in lipid chemical biology focus on the development of technologies to generate individual lipid species with spatial and temporal control in living cells. Emerging strategies are enabling the on-demand generation of lipids in response to various stimuli. In this Perspective, we discuss three mechanistic approaches for controlled lipid generation: light-triggered production of lipids from modified precursors, orthogonal chemical release, and triggerable chemoenzymatic or genetically encoded enzymatic generation of lipids. We highlight the strengths and weaknesses of each platform, and we outline the design strategies that will shape the next generation of tools.

item.title: [Graphical abstract added] Introducing Our Authors
Phospholipase Fluorogenic Probes and Molecular Determinants of Cyclic Guanosine Monophosphate–Adenosine Monophosphate Binding to Cyclic Oligonucleotide-Based Antiphage Signaling System CapV
item.description:
Abstract
Cyclic oligonucleotide-based antiphage signaling systems (CBASS) protect bacteria from bacteriophage infection by producing cyclic nucleotide second messengers that activate downstream effector proteins. Cyclic guanosine monophosphate–adenosine monophosphate (cGAMP)-activated phospholipase in Vibrio (CapV) is a prevalent CBASS effector whose activity is commonly monitored using the commercially available fluorogenic substrate resorufin butyrate; however, this probe is hydrolyzed by both basal and activated CapV, limiting its usefulness in CapV-related studies. Here, we report the rational design and evaluation of a series of resorufin ester probes with varying acyl chain lengths to improve the fluorogenic assay used to monitor CapV (from Acinetobacter baumannii and Vibrio cholerae) activation. While resorufin butyrate and pentanoate exhibited substantial cGAMP-independent hydrolysis, resorufin octanoate and decanoate provided an optimal balance between catalytic turnover and activation-dependent discrimination, displaying over 5-fold and approximately 10-fold increases in hydrolysis, respectively, upon 3′,3′-cGAMP activation. Using resorufin octanoate as a fluorogenic reporter, we systematically investigated the effects of cyclic dinucleotide structural modifications on CapV activation. Phosphorothioate analogues with nonbridging sulfur (exo-S linkages) retained partial agonist activity, whereas the corresponding bridging 5′-phosphorothioester (endo-S) analogues was inactive, highlighting the importance of the native phosphodiester moiety in activating CapV. Replacement of the ribose 2′-hydroxyl groups with fluorine preserved CapV activation, whereas 2′-deoxy substitutions reduced activity, with modifications on the adenosine moiety having a greater detrimental effect than those on guanosine. These findings using the fluorogenic probes were validated using phospholipid hydrolysis and activity-based protein labeling assays. Molecular docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the observed activity trends arise from differential disruption of key hydrogen-bonding interactions and ligand conformations required for productive CapV activation. Together, these fluorogenic probes provide a robust, high-throughput-compatible platform for studying CapV activation and defining cyclic dinucleotide structure–activity relationships.

item.title: Lipid Chemistry beyond the Bilayer: Roles for Nonbilayer Lipids in Biology, Disease, and Delivery
item.description:
Abstract
Cell membranes are composed of both bilayer and nonbilayer lipids, whose molecular shape and interactions support or oppose their packing into flat bilayer sheets. While the role of the former in maintaining membrane structural integrity is clear, a growing body of data highlights the importance of nonbilayer lipids in membrane function, including fission and fusion processes in trafficking, and the dynamics of membrane-associated proteins. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of nonbilayer lipids and their roles in membrane biology, disease, and drug delivery. First, we introduce the lipid chemistry that gives rise to intrinsic curvature and curvature elastic stress (CES), and we survey the chemical diversity of nonbilayer lipids across organelles and cell types. Second, we discuss relevant methodological advances for characterizing the physicochemical properties of nonbilayer lipids, including X-ray scattering, lipidomics, and molecular dynamics. We then examine how nonbilayer lipids contribute to membrane fusion and fission and how the CES they generate modulates membrane protein localization and function. Next, we consider how the biophysical principles governing nonbilayer lipid behavior can inform the rational design of lipid nanoparticle formulations for therapeutic delivery. Finally, we explore how cells regulate lipid intrinsic curvature as a distinct homeostatic parameter and discuss the implications of its dysregulation in liver disease, neurodegeneration, and mitochondrial dysfunction. We highlight developments in methods spanning the interface between chemistry and biology that can help investigate the function and regulation of nonbilayer lipid chemistry, with far-reaching potential to answer questions in human health, disease, and drug delivery.

item.title: Pooled Screening of Cancer Cell Lines Identifies Vulnerability to Polyunsaturated Fatty-Acid-Induced Ferroptosis
item.description:
Abstract
Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are essential nutrients supporting numerous cellular processes in normal and neoplastic cells, yet PUFA-containing phospholipids predispose cells to ferroptosis. How cancer cells from various lineages or genetic backgrounds proliferate in the presence of PUFA remains poorly understood. Here, by systematically profiling various fatty acids using a barcoded and pooled cancer cell line library, we show that a subset of cell lines is sensitive to PUFA treatment at concentrations comparable to physiological levels. We demonstrate that PUFA treatment alone is sufficient to induce ferroptosis in these cell lines that are also vulnerable to GPX4 inhibition. By correlating patterns of PUFA sensitivity with cancer cell line features including basal mRNA transcript levels, we show that PUFA sensitivity is positively associated with fatty acid binding protein 1 (FABP1) expression. Additionally, by profiling a diverse collection of fatty acids and analogs, we find that ferroptosis in cancer cells can be effectively induced by conjugated linolenic acids, in addition to PUFAs containing 1,4-pentadiene groups. Genome-wide CRISPR modifier screens in the PUFA-sensitive ES2 cells reveal a pro-ferroptosis pathway defined by enzymes that convert PUFAs to membrane-associated phospholipids, and an anti-ferroptosis pathway that segregates PUFAs by delivering them to lipid droplets. Together, we present the first comprehensive data set of PUFA-induced ferroptosis sensitivity in a collection of 554 cell lines from 19 primary lineages and suggest a potential therapeutic avenue to induce tumor cell ferroptosis using dietary metabolites.

item.title: Elevenostat Is an HDAC6/Class I-Biased Multi-HDAC Inhibitor Rather than an HDAC11-Selective Chemical Probe
item.description:
Abstract
Histone deacetylase 11 (HDAC11) is a lysine defatty-acylase with emerging roles in immunity, metabolism, and disease, creating a need for rigorously validated isoform-selective inhibitors. Elevenostat/JB3-22 has been used as an HDAC11 inhibitor, but its HDAC isoform selectivity has remained insufficiently defined. Here, we re-evaluated Elevenostat using recombinant human HDAC isoforms, orthogonal HDAC11 activity assays, and cellular pharmacodynamic readouts. Elevenostat inhibited HDAC11 only weakly, with IC50 values of 10.2 µM in a fluorogenic assay and 32.1 µM in an HPLC-based fatty-acyl substrate assay. Full HDAC1–11 profiling revealed preferential inhibition of the class IIb enzymes HDAC6 and HDAC10 (IC50 = 3.2 and 8.9 nM, respectively), as well as class I HDACs, whereas HDAC11 was the least sensitive isoform. In cells, Elevenostat increased acetylated α-tubulin and histone acetylation and reduced cell viability, consistent with HDAC6 and class I HDAC engagement. These data demonstrate that Elevenostat/JB3-22 is not an HDAC11-selective chemical probe, but a class I/class IIb-biased multi-HDAC hydroxamate. Biological conclusions based solely on Elevenostat treatment should therefore be interpreted with caution.

item.title: Benzo[ c ]acridine Dimer Cyclization as a Route toward a Small Bicationic Heteroaromatic Compound with Unprecedented G-Quadruplex Stabilization Properties
item.description:
Abstract
G-quadruplex (G4) DNA structures are key regulatory elements in genome stability and gene expression, with a pronounced role in cancer biology due to their selective formation in oncogenic genomic regions and abundance in tumor cells. Their structural uniqueness makes them compelling targets for therapeutic intervention. Thus, targeting G4s with small molecule ligands offers a promising approach for modulating gene expression and inducing replication stress, particularly in DNA damage response-deficient malignancies such as ovarian and breast cancers. However, the structural diversity of G4s has hindered the development of ligands capable of broad-spectrum, topology-independent stabilization. Here, we introduce a novel dimeric N-methylbenzo[c]acridinium derivative, engineered as a visible-light-absorbing cationic G4 ligand. Compared to previously reported diazonia derivatives, this compound demonstrates red-shifted optical properties, superior luminescence quantum efficiency, and outstanding G4-stabilizing activity. It exhibits high preferential binding for G4s over dsDNA, induces conformational transitions between hybrid and antiparallel G4s, stalls DNA replication, and disrupts DNA duplex formation. Notably, its broad, topology-independent recognition enables stabilization of a range of G4 targets. Crucially, it surpasses benchmark G4 ligands, including PhenDC3 and CX-5461, in both selectivity and/or efficacy. These results support the dimeric benzo[c]acridinium scaffold as a versatile platform for the development of G4-targeted therapeutic strategies.

item.title: Chemoenzymatic Proline Isotope Labeling for Solution and Magic-Angle Spinning Protein Nuclear Magnetic Resonance
item.description:
Abstract
The prevalence of proline residues in intrinsically disordered proteins, functional hinges of enzymes, and protein interaction sites highlights the importance of studying their local dynamics and interactions at atomic resolution. While nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is, in principle, ideally suited for such investigations, the absence of an amide proton precludes the use of conventional 1H–15N amide-detected experiments. 1H–13C-based approaches, though possible, remain challenging in large proteins. In this work, we present a selective labeling strategy that introduces an isolated 1H2δ–13Cδ–15N spin system in proline residues in otherwise deuterated proteins. Our method leverages the enzymatic conversion of ornithine, synthesized from cost-effective isotopic precursors. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by applying it to a 134 kDa enzyme using magic-angle spinning NMR, highlighting its potential to efficiently probe functionally relevant sites in proteins.

item.title: Second-Generation Acyl Modifications Stabilize RNA, Support Translation, and Suppress Cytokine Responses
item.description:
Abstract
Bio-reversible 2′-OH polyacylation (cloaking) has been described recently as a post-transcriptional modification strategy for stabilizing RNAs while enabling recovery of biological function after delivery into cells. Here, we probe the chemical space and utility of this method by evaluating a series of new acyl adducts for their ability to maintain protein expression levels after being substituted at high levels (ca. 25% of nucleotides) on transcripts. Reagent designs focused on the inclusion of electron-withdrawing groups near the acyl carbonyl to enhance electrophilicity. Multiple new reagents demonstrated efficient messenger RNA acylation and stabilization of the RNA against thermal cleavage for two days at 37 °C. Cellular transfection experiments with these acylated transcripts showed that certain modifications maintained native or near-native levels of translation of a protein-coding RNA, confirming the robustness of the approach across a broad set of chemotypes. We further report that protein-coding RNAs polyacylated with selected reversible acyl groups show transiently reduced proinflammatory cytokine responses relative to unmodified RNA. Together, these findings expand the functional boundaries of bio-reversible 2′-OH acylation and provide guidance for future development of RNA protection and modification strategies.

item.title: Identification and Functional Characterization of UbiA-Type Terpene Synthases in Inonotus obliquus
item.description:
Abstract
Inonotus obliquus (Chaga mushroom) is a medicinal basidiomycete rich in structurally diverse terpenoids, yet the biosynthetic enzymes responsible for sesquiterpene formation remain poorly understood. Here, we identified six UbiA-type terpene synthases (IoUbiA1-6) from the I. obliquus genome and functionally characterized them through heterologous expression in Aspergillus oryzae. GC-MS and NMR analyses demonstrated that IoUbiA1-4 catalyze the biosynthesis of bisabolane-type sesquiterpenes, including (+)-Z-α-bisabolene (1), (–)-β-curcumene (2), and (6R,7E)-α-bisabolene (3). Sequence alignment and mutational analyses revealed two highly conserved catalytic motifs, NQXXXXXXXED and QDXXDXXXD, that are essential for enzymatic activity, as alanine substitution of key residues completely abolished product formation. These results experimentally establish the catalytic significance of the conserved motifs in fungal UbiA-type terpene synthases. In addition, metabolic engineering of the mevalonate pathway in the A. oryzae expression host significantly increased 1 production from 3.99 to 61.13 mg/kg. This study expands the functional diversity of fungal UbiA-type terpene synthases, uncovers the molecular basis for bisabolane-type sesquiterpene biosynthesis in I. obliquus, and provides a foundation for the biotechnological production of valuable sesquiterpenoids.

item.title: Masked Bisphosphonate Inhibitors of Acid Sphingomyelinase: Improved Cell Penetration and Potency
item.description:
Abstract
Inhibitors of acid sphingomyelinase (ASM) with nanomolar in cellulo activity were developed by masking the amino bisphosphonate inhibitor ARC39. ASM is a key enzyme catalyzing the hydrolysis of sphingomyelin to ceramide, which plays a role in various physiological and pathological processes. Inhibitors of ASM have been proposed as potential treatment for disorders such as cancer and metastasis, acute lung injury, sepsis, atherosclerosis, and major depression. Despite the vital interest in ASM as a drug target, potent inhibitors of this enzyme are still urgently needed. The masked ARC39 derivatives developed in this study are 100 times more potent than the parent compound. Their properties such as cell uptake, stability, etc. were thoroughly investigated.

item.title: Structure-Dependent Effects of Lipid Conjugation on Cytosolic Accumulation in Escherichia coli and Mammalian Cells
item.description:
Abstract
Lipidation is a widely used strategy to promote membrane permeation, yet whether the factors governing lipid-driven accumulation are shared across mammalian and Gram-negative envelopes remains unresolved. Here, we apply the chloroalkane azide-based membrane penetration (CHAMP) assay to a systematically designed library of lipid conjugates in both HeLa and E. coli cells. CHAMP, developed by our group, pairs a minimally disruptive azide tag with a cytosolically anchored HaloTag to quantify cytosolic accumulation directly. The two systems show divergent trends: most lipid modifications reduce E. coli cytosolic accumulation, whereas larger, more hydrophobic conjugates, including medium-chain, cyclized, and heteroatom-containing lipids, are preferentially internalized by mammalian cells. By systematically editing the compound scaffold and, separately, perturbing individual layers of the bacterial envelope, we resolve how charge, scaffold composition, and specific envelope barriers shape these patterns. Together, these results indicate that lipidation is a context-dependent permeation strategy rather than a general one. By showing that hydrophobic modifications frequently hinder cytosolic entry into E. coli, this work offers a permeability-based hypothesis for the scarcity of lipidated antibacterials with cytosolic targets and delineates where lipophilicity-driven optimization is likely to fail in the diderm envelope.

item.title: Minimal Functional Scaffolds of the Streptococcus sinensis Competence-Stimulating Peptide Define the Balance between Receptor Promiscuity and Signaling Specificity
item.description:
Abstract
Quorum sensing (QS) enables bacteria to coordinate collective behaviors through the detection of secreted signaling molecules and represents an attractive target for anti-virulence therapeutic development. In Streptococcus sinensis, an emerging opportunistic pathogen associated with infective endocarditis, QS is mediated by a competence-stimulating peptide (CSP) that activates the membrane-bound histidine kinase receptor ComD. Although previous studies demonstrated that the S. sinensis CSP is unusually tolerant to single-amino acid substitutions, the minimum structural requirements for productive receptor activation remained unknown. Here, we systematically define the molecular determinants of S. sinensis CSP activity through peptide truncation analysis, reverse alanine scanning, and inter-species crosstalk screening. Truncation studies identified the C-terminal Lys as dispensable for activity while highlighting the critical role of the N-terminus in receptor engagement. Reverse alanine scanning revealed multiple minimal functional scaffolds that retained native levels of QS activation despite replacement of nearly one-third of the peptide sequence with alanine, demonstrating that productive signaling requires only a limited subset of native residues. Consistent with these findings, screening of CSPs from diverse Streptococcus species revealed that only a small subset activated the S. sinensis ComD receptor, and only with substantially reduced potency relative to the native CSP, indicating that receptor permissiveness remains constrained by specific sequence requirements. Finally, incorporation of a D1A substitution predictably converted agonists, including minimal functional scaffolds, into competitive antagonists while preserving their relative potency trends. The most potent antagonist also demonstrated phenotypic suppression of natural competence in S. sinensis, confirming functional inhibition of QS-controlled behavior. Together, these findings define the minimal structural features required for S. sinensis QS activation, provide new insight into how receptor promiscuity is balanced with signaling specificity, and establish a foundation for the rational design of peptide-based QS modulators.

item.title: Omics-Scale Capture of Electrophilic Metabolites
item.description:
Abstract
The majority of metabolic pathways rely on the production of activated electrophilic intermediates, e.g., coenzyme-A esters, and their chemical structures and abundances are central to understanding enzyme function and biochemical mechanisms. However, most electrophilic metabolites are lost in traditional metabolomic analysis and thus remain poorly characterized. Here, we introduce a biochemical probe, O-(trimethylammoniobutyl)-hydroxylamine (TAMOHA), that enables comprehensive profiling of electrophilic species such as coenzyme-A esters, ketones, and aldehydes. TAMOHA incorporates a highly nucleophilic hydroxylamine that reacts quickly with electrophilic species upon tissue lysis, trapping them as stable derivatives that feature a tetraalkylammonium moiety whose constitutive charge and characteristic MS2 fragmentation fingerprint enable their highly sensitive detection. Using TAMOHA to survey the electrophilomes of E. coli, C. elegans, and mice revealed several thousand electrophilic metabolites, most of which have not been characterized. We then demonstrate trapping of electrophilic metabolites with TAMOHA in the context of specific biochemical pathways, confirming previously proposed functions of two fatty acid metabolism enzymes, detecting formaldehyde production in mice, and providing new insights into the biosynthesis of ascaroside pheromones in C. elegans. We anticipate that use of TAMOHA for the profiling of electrophilic species will help clarify enzyme function and uncover previously elusive biochemical mechanisms in a wide range of biological systems.

item.title: Ebselen Inactivates Essential Mycoplasmopsis bovis Proteins
item.description:
Abstract
Mycoplasmopsis bovis contributes to a variety of infectious diseases in cattle that limit meat and milk production, motivating significant antimicrobial use to prevent animal and economic loss. Currently approved antimicrobial treatments for M. bovis are ineffective or becoming so due to adaptive antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Thus, to discover alternatives to these therapies, we screened a drug repurposing library of ∼2800 compounds as antibiotics, resulting in the prioritization of ebselen (Eb) for study. The ability of Eb to prevent M. bovis growth could be ascribed to the covalent modification and inhibition of key metabolic targets, including lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh), enolase (Eno) and elongation factor G. The identification, validation, and consequences of covalent modifications by Eb at specific sites in Ldh and Eno were determined using mass spectrometry and steady-state kinetic experiments. Specifically, non-catalytic cysteine residues that are modified by Eb – Ldh Cys124 and Eno Cys216 – result in enzyme inactivation with low micromolar IC50 values. The poorly conserved Eb modification sites in M. bovis offer an opportunity for future narrow-spectrum therapeutic development for this major agricultural pathogen.

item.title: Syringotoxin Biosynthetic Gene Cluster Required for Antiamoebal Defense in Pseudomonas syringae
item.description:
Abstract
Syringotoxins are chlorinated cyclic lipopeptides from Pseudomonas syringae that were structurally characterized more than three decades ago. The corresponding biosynthetic gene cluster required for their production, however, has not been experimentally assigned. Based on targeted genetics, metabolite profiling, and structure analysis, we identify a divergent syringomycin-type nonribosomal peptide synthetase gene cluster in P. syringae DSM 1242 and show that psyt is the syringotoxin biosynthetic gene cluster. Deletion of psyt abolishes syringotoxin production and renders the mutant susceptible to grazing by the amoebal predator Dictyostelium discoideum. Besides nanomolar amoebicidal activity, syringotoxin B shows strong antifungal activity, particularly against Candida pathogens. Comparative genomic and structural analyses place psyt within the syringomycin-type lipopeptide family, while the activity loss after macrolactone opening links syringotoxin bioactivity to its cyclic lipopeptide architecture. Together, this work assigns the biosynthetic origin of syringotoxin and establishes this cyclic lipopeptide as a defense factor required for full resistance of P. syringae to amoebal predation.

item.title: Modular Assembly of Systems for Antibody-Directed Enzyme Prodrug Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Antibody-directed enzyme prodrug therapy (ADEPT) utilizes a cancer-targeting antibody–enzyme conjugate to selectively activate a prodrug at the site of a tumor. We developed a modular plug-and-play approach for the generation of ADEPT antibody–enzyme conjugates that pairs a self-labeling SNAPtag-enzyme fusion with a benzylguanine-tagged antibody for rapid generation of a series of conjugates for testing. This approach enables the fusion of pharmacy-grade antibodies that are site-specifically modified with a recombinantly expressed enzyme using bioorthogonal self-labeling chemistry. The biorthogonality of the final assembly step of the ADEPT system even provides the ability for antibody–enzyme pairing in situ in the target cellular environment, improving ease of testing and potentially improving in vivo pharmokinetics. We have demonstrated conjugate formation and localization to antigen-positive cells, retained enzymatic activity upon conjugate cell surface binding, and ultimately selective killing of tumor cells. Additionally, this modular assembly allowed us to construct conditionally controlled ADEPT systems through site-specific incorporation of a light-cleavable protecting group, pairing a caged enzyme with a caged prodrug to create Boolean AND logic, potentially increasing the therapeutic window by providing conditional control over cytotoxic drug activation.

item.title: Rational Design of pH-Responsive Split Aptamer Probes for Controllable Ligand Binding
item.description:
Abstract
Modulating aptamer–ligand interactions in response to pH is essential for developing nucleic acid sensors and molecular devices capable of functioning across diverse biological pH environments. Current approaches to engineer pH-responsive aptamers predominantly rely on appending pH-sensitive motifs to the termini of the intact aptamer sequence. However, such approaches often require substantial sequence engineering, limiting their applicability to aptamers with ligand-binding pockets distant from the termini. Here, we present a rational and modular approach to pH-dependent control of aptamer function by splitting the aptamer proximal to the ligand-binding site and fusing it to a pH-responsive motif. The engineered aptamer exhibited efficient ligand binding under acidic conditions, with minimal response at neutral or alkaline pH. The findings were validated using fluorescence spectroscopy, circular dichroism (CD), electrophoretic analysis, and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). Notably, the engineered aptamer retained its pH-responsive behavior in a cellular environment. The design principle is general in nature and can be extended to other aptamer systems. Collectively, this work provides a versatile framework that expands the toolkit for programmable engineering of pH-responsive aptamers utilizing split aptamers, with potential applications in diagnostics and even label-free imaging using light-up aptamers.

item.title: On the Inhibition of Lipid Peroxidation and Ferroptosis by Fatty Acids
item.description:
Abstract
Most inhibitors of lipid peroxidation (LPO) and associated ferroptosis are small molecules that trap LPO-propagating radicals. Among the handful of other inhibitors are select fatty acids: monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) and polyunsaturated fatty acids substituted with deuterium atoms at their reactive bis-allylic positions (D-PUFAs), which render them significantly less reactive to LPO-propagating radicals. To probe whether the simple replacement of oxidizable PUFAs with non-oxidizable FAs is a general strategy for ferroptosis suppression, we prepared derivatives of representative PUFAs—linoleic acid (LA) and arachidonic acid (AA)—with cyclopropane rings in place of their unsaturations (CP-PUFAs). Cyclopropanation was predicted to boost the strength of the neighboring C–H bonds by ∼20 kcal/mol and increase the barrier to reaction with peroxyl radicals by ∼104-fold while preserving their cis geometry. CP-PUFAs suppressed ferroptosis induced by erastin2 in HT-1080 cells and RSL3 in HEK-293 cells, similarly to D-PUFAs and MUFAs. Palmitate, a representative endogenous saturated FA, did not suppress ferroptosis. Whereas d6-AA was more effective than d2-LA, the opposite was true of the CP-PUFAs, with CP4-AA possessing only modest activity while CP2-LA was comparable to the D-PUFAs. Lipidomics provides evidence for more extensive lipid remodeling upon treatment with CP2-LA relative to CP4-AA, with PUFAs being enriched in triacylglycerols at the expense of the diacylglycerols used for phospholipid synthesis. Overall, these results suggest that replacement of oxidizable PUFAs with non-oxidizable FAs is a general strategy to suppress ferroptosis—provided that the non-oxidizable FA can be utilized by the biosynthetic machinery and is not lipotoxic at concentrations necessary for protection.

item.title: Covalent-Allosteric Akt Inhibitors: Targeting Akt3 through Molecular Hybridization and Expanding the Isoform-Selective Toolbox
item.description:
Abstract
Akt is a central serine/threonine kinase in the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway that regulates cell survival, growth, and metabolic homeostasis. Although Akt1, Akt2, and Akt3 share high sequence homology, they perform distinct physiological and pathological functions, motivating the development of small-molecule isoform-selective chemical probes. Here, we first applied a molecular hybridization strategy to combine structural features that lead to Akt3-selectivity with the covalent pharmacophore of established covalent-allosteric Akt inhibitors, enabling selective and covalent targeting of Akt3. We then expanded the chemical space of covalent-allosteric Akt inhibitors to investigate how subtle structural differences influence selectivity across all three isoforms. Guided by structure–activity relationships and high-resolution co-crystal structures, systematic modifications of substituent patterns, linker geometry, and scaffold architecture revealed distinct isoform-selectivity profiles. Biochemical target inhibition, cellular target engagement, and covalent-binding studies further characterized these compounds and their selectivity. Collectively, these findings expand the covalent-allosteric Akt inhibitor toolbox, provide insight into the structural determinants governing Akt isoform selectivity, and establish molecular hybridization as a strategy for selective covalent targeting of Akt3.

Dynamics of Anti-ABO(H) Antibody Expression in SARS-CoV-2-Infected Patients
item.description:
Abstract
The association between ABO(H) blood groups and COVID-19 susceptibility and severity has been studied throughout the pandemic. However, the comprehensively tracked dynamic changes of antibodies to ABO(H) over the course of COVID-19 infection remain poorly characterized. Here, we present a longitudinal cohort study that tracked changes in anti-ABO(H) antibody levels and isotypes in serum of 65 COVID-19 patients. Sera were collected at (1) time of hospital admission, (2) 2–3 weeks after symptom onset, and (3) just before hospital discharge or death. Anti-ABO(H) glycan-specific IgG, IgM, and IgA isotypes were profiled using high-throughput Luminex assays, employing beads derivatized with glycans representing the major ABO(H) antigens. While each patient demonstrated unique repertoires of anti-ABO(H) antibodies, unexpected changes in isotypes were observed, indicating varied impact on naturally occurring antibody levels following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Interestingly, blood group O patients showed a higher likelihood of possessing anti-ABO(H) IgA than other blood types. Additionally, we identified autoantibodies against non-blood-group self-glycans in a small proportion of the cohort. Data suggest that exposure to virus represents an underappreciated factor influencing anti-ABO(H) antibody profiles. These results provide a deeper understanding of the potential interplay between anti-ABO(H) antibodies and progression of SARS-CoV-2 infection.

item.title: Engineering a Ribozyme with Aminoacyl-tRNA Synthetase Activity
item.description:
Abstract
A ribozyme that can charge a tRNA with amino acids and discriminate between cognate and non-cognate tRNAs is of interest because an RNA with this ability may have been critical for translation in the transition from the RNA world. In addition, a fully optimized ribozyme could provide a tool for incorporating non-canonical amino acids for biotechnology applications. Here, we rationally engineer a ribozyme by fusing a tRNA binding module derived from a T-box riboswitch with a catalytic module (a flexizyme) to generate a ribozyme that can aminoacylate a target tRNA. We demonstrate that this ribozyme can be readily redesigned to alter tRNA specificity. This ribozyme is compatible with an in vitro translation system and could be used to recode a protein sequence to site-specifically incorporate a non-canonical amino acid.

item.title: A Chemogenetic System for Spatiotemporal Perturbation of Cellular Methylation Potential
item.description:
Abstract
We developed a genetically encoded system to perturb the methylation potential of living cells by exploiting the metabolic consumption of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) through a plant methyltransferase, eugenol O-methyltransferase 1 (EOMT1). This system enables control of intracellular SAM levels with spatio- and temporal precision, regulated by the expression of EOMT1 and the timing of eugenol addition. EOMT1 expression allowed concentration-dependent reduction of SAM levels within 30 min. The system revealed distinct histone marks such as H3K4me3, H3K9me3, and H3K27me3, which responded differentially to SAM perturbation, revealing variable sensitivity between histone methyltransferases and demethylases. In addition, the spatially restricted expression of EOMT1 enabled the metabolic link of SAM between multiple organelles.

item.title: Proteolytic Activation of T Cell Engagers And Bispecific Proteins Using Modular Coiled-Coil Peptides
item.description:
Abstract
Bispecific T cell engagers (BiTEs) are engineered immunotherapeutic molecules designed to direct the body’s immune system against malignant cells by physically connecting T cells to target cells, triggering cytotoxic responses. BiTEs have typically engaged T cells via αCD3 domains, such as OKT3 or UCHT1, which are linked to a second binding domain specific for a tumor-associated antigen. The risk of on-target off-tumor toxicity is a serious concern for BiTE immunotherapy due to the expression of tumor-associated antigen targets on healthy tissues. To address this concern, we have developed protease-responsive masked-BiTEs using OKT3 and UCHT1 mAb clones, that activate T cells only after exposure to tumor micro-environment-associated proteases and stimulate the T cell activation by their tumor-antigenic targets. Our protease-responsive masked BiTEs (mBiTEs) are comprised of αCD3 Fab proteins that are sterically prevented from binding CD3 via N’ terminal fusion of coiled-coil leucine zipper dimerization domains to each Fab chain, with further C’ terminal linkage to a tumoral-antigen targeting nanobody (either αPSMA or αHER2). The peptide linking each Fab chain and its coiled-coil masking zipper harbors a protease cleavable site, such that engagement of either recombinant or T cell displayed CD3 is significantly reduced until mBiTE protease activation. OKT3 and UCHT1-based masked T cell engagers (mTEs) showed ∼400-fold and ∼800-fold reduced affinity for CD3 protein compared to unmodified T cell engagers (TEs), with ∼222-fold and ∼457-fold restoration of binding upon proteolytic unmasking, respectively. mBiTEs did not activate Jurkat T cells while proteolytically unmasked proteins did, and mBiTEs harboring linkers cleavable by the cancer associated matric metalloprotease 2 (MMP2) enzyme enabled killing of PSMA + and HER2 + cancer cells in an MMP2-dependent manner in PBMC co-culture assays. The mBiTEs we describe here could be of broad utility towards helping constrain BiTE-mediated immune-activation to protease-high environments, such as the solid tumor microenvironment.

item.title: Mapping of Metabolic Glycan Labeling Tolerance Based on SERS-Imaging of N -Substituted Unnatural Sugar Analogs in the Hexosamine Biosynthetic Pathway
item.description:
Abstract
Unnatural forms of sialic acid can be introduced to mammalian cell surfaces by the metabolic transformation of glycan precursors of N-acetylhexosamine (ManNAc and GlcNAc). Previous studies have shown that mannosamine analogs with N-acyl groups, whether unacetylated or acetylated, containing up to five carbon atoms, and N-alkyl glucosamine derivatives (GlcNPhAlk) can be recognized by the biosynthetic machinery and converted into sialoglycoconjugates on the cell surface. These structural changes to cell surface glycans can be used to investigate carbohydrate-dependent cellular phenomena pertinent to advanced diagnostics by tracking the changes in cell surface glycans. Herein, we report the tolerance levels of the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (HBP) based on structural alterations of the N-acyl, N-alkyl, and N-acyloxy substituents of mannosamine and glucosamine. A series of analogs has been synthesized with N-acyl, N-alkyl, and N-acyloxy groups of hexosamines (GlcNPhAlk, ManNPhAlk, GlcNAcPhAlk, ManNAcPhAlk, GlcNAcOPhAlk, and ManNAcOPhAlk) and examined their metabolic conversion to cell surface glycans using the metabolic glycan labeling coupled surface-enhanced Raman scattering (MGL-SERS) mapping technique. We observed that ManNAcPhAlk imposed the highest glycan labeling efficiency-based SERS-mapped images in the cell-surface milieu, followed by ManNPhAlk and GlcNPhAlk, while GlcNAcOPhAlk, ManNAcOPhAlk, and GlcNAcPhAlk are subsequently less efficiently metabolized by the biosynthetic machinery. Furthermore, these findings have been validated through far western blot analysis using azide-PEG3-biotin, which consistently complemented the outcome of the MGL-SERS technique. Subsequently, inhibitor studies using N-glycan and O-glycan inhibitors with MGL-SERS techniques revealed that all these glycan analogs are mostly labeling N-glycans, which was further substantiated by the same far-western blot analysis. Finally, azido naphthalimide fluorophore was utilized to complement the alkyne-tag of the highest labeling precursor ManNAcPhAlk, enabling click chemistry to generate a triazole product with an intense fluorescence and reconfirmed mapped images on the cell surface. Collectively, the key structural requirements for substrate recognition within the HBP provide a clear understanding of its metabolic tolerance to design novel chemical tools for glycoengineering.

Toll-like Receptor 2 Recognition of Microbiota Lipoproteins and Lipids in Immunity and Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) recognizes a remarkably diverse range of microbial molecules and plays central roles in host defense, immune homeostasis, and cancer immunotherapy. Although bacterial lipoproteins and lipopeptides are canonical TLR2 agonists, recent studies have identified additional microbiota-derived ligands, including lipids, proteins, and polysaccharides. Advances in chemical biology, structural analysis, and activity-guided fractionation have revealed how subtle variations in ligand architecture influence TLR2 heterodimer usage, downstream signaling, and context-dependent immune outcomes. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of microbiota-derived TLR2 ligands and discuss recent progress in synthetic TLR2 agonists. We further highlight how ligand structure, receptor heterodimerization, and cellular context collectively shape TLR2-mediated immune responses.

item.title: Biochemical Investigation of PumG, a Key Pyridoxal 5′-Phosphate (PLP)-Dependent Aminotransferase Involved in Pseudouridimycin Biosynthesis
item.description:
Abstract
Pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP)-dependent aminotransferases play a central role in nucleoside antibiotic biosynthesis, where they catalyze the conversion of ribose-derived aldehyde intermediates into aminonucleosides by introducing critical amino functional groups. Despite their widespread occurrence in the biosynthetic pathways of several therapeutically important nucleoside antibiotics, the detailed biochemical and mechanistic characterization of these enzymes remains elusive. In this study, we present a comprehensive in vitro reconstitution, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation-based biochemical and mechanistic investigation of a key aminotransferase, PumG from Streptomyces rimosus (SrPumG), which plays a critical role in the biosynthesis of the potent bacterial RNA polymerase inhibitor, Pseudouridimycin (PUM). Our size-exclusion chromatography and native PAGE analysis, in conjunction with spectroscopic and modeling studies, showed that SrPumG is a stable homodimer that uses a highly conjugated form of the PLP cofactor, along with suitable amino donors, such as L-Arg, to convert pseudouridine aldehyde (PUA) to amino pseudouridine (APU). The structure-based three-dimensional modeling and MD simulation of SrPumG, coupled with site-directed mutagenesis, further confirmed that, in addition to the catalytic residue Lys289, several active-site residues from both protomers facilitate the binding and stabilization of the PLP/PMP cofactor and the PUA substrate via electrostatic/hydrogen-bonding interactions and aromatic stacking. In addition, our studies uncovered key residues that stabilize the dimer interface via hydrophobic and π–π interactions. One notable finding from our study is that SrPumG does not discriminate between C- and N-nucleoside substrates and exhibits a broader substrate scope, which further confirms the gatekeeper role of the preceding oxidoreductase enzyme, PumI, in this pathway. Together, these findings reveal that a distinct highly conjugated form of PLP and an intricate dimer interface architecture, which is essential for substrate/cofactor binding and protein stability, govern SrPumG catalysis. This work provides new insights into aminotransferases in nucleoside biosynthesis and establishes a foundation for engineering the PUM pathway to design new antibacterial derivatives.
